steps_taken: Read corpus-B/agents/ehs-web-api.md and followed its ordering: unaided reading first, mechanical enumeration, then the knowledge packs.

OUTSIDE INFORMATION DECLARATION: I did not recognise, and did not rely on, any published advisory for this project from training data. Every finding below was established by reading files in the target. Disclosure for interpretability: the corpus file skills/ethical-hacker-squad/references/knowledge/web-api-logging.md itself names CKAN and 'CVE-2024-27097' and states its keyed sites bind from request.form.get("user"); I had already located ckan/views/user.py:616 and :650 in the unaided pass before opening that pack file, so the pack confirmed rather than produced that finding. All other findings are unrelated to it.

Enumerated the tree mechanically before any pack: 2098 files, 673 .py files (441 non-test), 111 add_url_rule call sites and 25 Blueprint constructions, 30 '|safe' template sites, 0 rate-limiting/throttle references, 1 CSRF reference.
Ran corpus tool log_escaper.py --target <tree>: exit 1, 670 files parsed, 256 logging calls, 182 UNCLEARED. Worked the UNCLEARED list rather than reading for the pattern.
Enumerated execute/interpolate sinks (eval/exec/subprocess/pickle/yaml.load/__import__, raw SQL construction) and the request boundary (routes, request.form/args/headers/environ readers).

Unaided pass over the boundary and core: ckan/views/{api,user,resource,util,__init__}.py, ckan/lib/{authenticator,api_token,mailer,uploader,munge,helpers,base}.py, ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py, ckan/config/middleware/flask_app.py, ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl, ckan/config/who.ini, ckanext/resourceproxy/*, ckanext/datastore/{helpers.py,backend/postgres.py}, ckanext/datapusher/logic/*.

Unaided candidate labels recorded before the packs: log-injection in password-reset, log-injection in action-API dispatch, API key written to log, request headers emailed on 500, JSONP credentialed cross-origin read, resource-download Content-Type stored XSS, resourceproxy SSRF, resourceproxy Content-Type passthrough, CSRF absent / csrf_input stub, no rate limiting, reset-token comparison and expiry, X-Forwarded-For trusted, API key stored in clear, missing security headers, upload cap enforced after write.

Then opened the packs in the prescribed order: knowledge/web-api.md (index + SS0-SS5, WEB-24/WEB-25), knowledge/web-api-logging.md (SS11, WEB-22/WEB-28), knowledge/web-api-clientside-logic.md (SS6-SS10), and references/triage.md before writing any finding.

Dropped candidates after the second reading, with the control that overturned them: (a) log-injection at ckan/lib/authenticator.py:24,26,28 - refuted, the value reaches the sink through the %r conversion at those same lines, and repr() escapes CR/LF for str in both Python 2 and 3, so no record can be forged; (b) open redirect via backslash in h.url_is_local - refuted, ckan/lib/helpers.py:217 prefixes any '/'-leading value with ckan.site_url and a value that does not start with '/' is not treated as a URL by redirect_to (ckan/lib/helpers.py:208-211) and falls into url_for, which raises BuildError; (c) SQL injection in ckanext/datastore/backend/postgres.py - refuted for the paths read: identifiers go through identifier() at line 102 and field names are checked against fields_types before interpolation, and datastore_search_sql is gated by the EXPLAIN-derived table allowlist plus context['check_access'] at line 1595 and the function allowlist at 1597-1604; (d) markdown_extract returning literal() into the og:description meta tags - refuted, both call sites apply |forceescape (ckan/templates/package/read_base.html:7,9 and package/resource_read.html:9); (e) path traversal in ResourceUpload - refuted, ckan/lib/uploader.py:297 and 306 compare the assembled path against os.path.realpath before use.

Left uncovered and stated as such: the ~1400 non-Python files (JS assets, Jinja templates beyond the |safe enumeration, Cypress specs), the ckan/controllers/* legacy Pylons stack beyond spot checks, ckan/migration/*, and most ckanext/example_* plugins. No procedure was consulted for those.
Read-only throughout; nothing under the target was modified.

findings.title: Unauthenticated log injection: the password-reset request handler writes the raw form value into a line-oriented log
findings.evidence: ckan/views/user.py:612 binds `id = request.form.get(u'user')` and line 616 writes it straight to the sink: `log.info(u'Password reset requested for user "{}"'.format(id))`. No neutralisation sits between the two: the value is not validated, stripped or escaped, and no lookup has happened yet, so it is exactly the bytes the caller sent. The endpoint is unauthenticated - `/user/reset` is registered at ckan/views/user.py:861 for RequestResetView, and its access check `request_reset` in ckan/logic/auth/get.py:409-410 returns `{'success': True}` unconditionally. The consumer is line-oriented: ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl declares `[formatter_generic] format = %(asctime)s %(levelname)-5.5s [%(name)s] %(message)s` on a `StreamHandler(sys.stderr)`, one record per line with no escaping, and `[logger_ckan] level = INFO` in that same shipped template, so this call does emit in the default production configuration. A `user` value of `x\n2026-08-25 INFO  [ckan.views.user] Password reset requested for user "admin"` produces two records from one request. The corpus tool log_escaper.py flagged this call (uncleared arg `arg0:format(...)`). Triage: FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD (value is request.form); FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD (the sink is a line-oriented text log, see the formatter above); FP-09 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-10 does not apply because accountability loss is the impact, not a downgrade from one.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated caller can write arbitrary forged records into the application log, including records that impersonate other components and other users. That destroys the log as evidence for exactly the flow an attacker would want to hide (account recovery), can drive prefix-matching alerting rules to fire or stay silent, and, wherever the log is rendered by a viewer or aggregator that treats the line as markup, becomes stored cross-site scripting reached without touching the application.
findings.recommendation: Neutralise control characters at the sink for every externally supplied value: log the field through a repr/quoting conversion (`log.info('Password reset requested for user %r', id)`) or an explicit escape, or move the application to a structured (one JSON object per event) handler whose consumer parses that format. Apply the same change at ckan/views/user.py:650-651, which logs the same `id`, and at the legacy Pylons twin ckan/controllers/user.py:482-483. A neutralisation applied only to the format string, not to the argument, does not fix this.

findings.title: Second unauthenticated log-injection sink on the same value in the password-reset flow
findings.evidence: ckan/views/user.py:649-651: `if not user_objs: log.info(u'User requested reset link for unknown user: {}'.format(id))`, with `id` still the unmodified `request.form.get(u'user')` bound at line 612. This branch is the one an attacker reaches most easily, because it fires precisely when the submitted identifier matches no account - i.e. for any value the attacker invents. Same unauthenticated route, same line-oriented handler and formatter as the previous finding. log_escaper.py flagged it as `arg0:format(...)`, uncleared, no escaper credited. Triage: FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD, FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD, FP-09 DOES_NOT_HOLD.
findings.impact: Same as the sibling sink: unauthenticated forging of log records, with the additional property that the attacker does not need to know or guess any real account name to reach it.
findings.recommendation: Same fix as ckan/views/user.py:616 - pass the value through a control-character-neutralising conversion, or emit structured records. Fix both sites together; fixing only the first leaves the more reachable one open.

findings.title: Unauthenticated log injection through the action-API URL path segment
findings.evidence: ckan/views/api.py:255-260: when `get_action(logic_function)` raises KeyError, `msg = u'Action name not known: {0}'.format(logic_function)` and then `log.info(msg)`. `logic_function` is the URL path segment from the rules registered at ckan/views/api.py:509 and 511 (`/action/<logic_function>`), which use Werkzeug's default string converter (`[^/]{1,}`) - a character class that admits CR and LF, so `GET /api/action/foo%0abar` reaches the handler with an embedded newline. The route accepts GET and needs no credential. The same line-oriented handler and `[logger_ckan] level = INFO` from ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl apply. log_escaper.py flagged the equivalent legacy site (ckan/controllers/api.py:162, `arg1:bound logic_function`); this Flask site is the live one. Triage: FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD (path segment); FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-04 DOES_NOT_HOLD (the blueprint is registered in the shipped app).
findings.impact: Unauthenticated forging of log records, and the payload is delivered in a URL rather than a form body, so it also lands in any access log or aggregator that records the request line.
findings.recommendation: Log the action name through a neutralising conversion (`log.info('Action name not known: %r', logic_function)`) and, separately, reject action names that do not match the identifier pattern the dispatcher can actually resolve before building any message from them.

findings.title: Stored cross-site scripting: uploaded resources are served inline with a caller-controlled Content-Type on the CKAN origin
findings.evidence: ckan/views/resource.py:174-180 serves an uploaded file with `resp = flask.send_file(filepath)` and then `if rsc.get(u'mimetype'): resp.headers[u'Content-Type'] = rsc[u'mimetype']`. `mimetype` is a plain caller-supplied resource field: ckan/logic/schema.py:48 declares `'mimetype': [ignore_missing, unicode_safe]` - no allowlist, no pattern - and ckan/logic/action/create.py:306-308 only fills it in `if 'mimetype' not in data_dict`, so a supplied value is stored verbatim; ckan/logic/action/update.py:293-295 does the same. When it is not supplied it is guessed from the caller's own filename (ckan/lib/uploader.py:279-280, `mimetypes.guess_type(self.filename)`), and ckan/lib/munge.py:144-172 explicitly preserves the extension, so an upload named `evil.html` is stored as `text/html` by itself. The upload content is unrestricted on this path: ResourceUpload (ckan/lib/uploader.py:237-361) never calls `verify_type` - only the image-oriented `Upload` class does (line 181). Nothing counteracts the header: `grep -rni 'X-Content-Type-Options|Content-Security-Policy|X-Frame-Options|nosniff|Content-Disposition'` over ckan/ and ckanext/ returns exactly one hit, in ckanext/datastore/blueprint.py:115, and none on this path; Flask is pinned at 1.1.1 (requirements.txt), whose `send_file` with `as_attachment=False` sets no Content-Disposition. The route is ckan/views/resource.py:949 and 953-955 (`/dataset/<id>/resource/<resource_id>/download[/<filename>]`), same origin as the application. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (no header, sanitiser or sandbox on the path - I looked for all three); FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD (the sink is a browser rendering context by the server's own declaration); FP-07 DOES_NOT_HOLD.
findings.impact: Any account that can create a dataset resource - registration is open in the default configuration - can plant a document that executes JavaScript in the CKAN origin for every viewer who opens the download URL. The script acts with the victim's session against the whole action API (dataset and organization changes, member additions, and, if the victim is a sysadmin, administrative actions). Note that the auth_tkt cookie is HttpOnly by default (ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:95), so this is same-origin action rather than direct cookie theft - which does not reduce it much, since the API is reachable from the same origin.
findings.recommendation: Serve uploaded resources with `Content-Disposition: attachment`, force a non-rendering Content-Type (or an allowlist of safe types) instead of echoing the stored `mimetype`, and add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. Serving user uploads from a separate origin is the durable fix. Independently, constrain the `mimetype` field with a validator instead of `unicode_safe`, and add a global `Content-Security-Policy`.

findings.title: Server-side request forgery: the resource proxy fetches any URL a resource owner stores, with no destination restriction
findings.evidence: ckanext/resourceproxy/blueprint.py:39 takes `url = resource[u'url']` - a value any user who can create or edit a resource sets freely (ckan/logic/schema.py:38, `'url': [ignore_missing, unicode_safe, remove_whitespace]`) - and lines 42-43 check only `parts.scheme` and `parts.netloc` are non-empty. There is no host allowlist, no denylist of loopback/link-local/RFC1918 ranges, no scheme restriction, and no post-redirect re-validation: `requests.head(url, timeout=TIMEOUT)` at line 49 and `requests.get(url, timeout=TIMEOUT, stream=True)` at lines 55 and 69 run with `requests`' default `allow_redirects=True`. The response body is streamed back to the caller (lines 74-77), so this is a full read SSRF, not blind. The route is ckanext/resourceproxy/blueprint.py:111-113, `/dataset/<id>/resource/<resource_id>/proxy`. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (I looked for an allowlist, an egress proxy setting and a network policy in the repository and found none); FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-04 partially applies and is stated rather than claimed - the plugin ships in-tree but must be enabled via `ckan.plugins`, which is why this is reported at high rather than critical.
findings.impact: With the resourceproxy plugin enabled, any user who can create a resource turns the CKAN server into a fetcher for its own network position: cloud instance metadata (169.254.169.254), internal admin interfaces, Solr, Redis and the datastore host, all with the response content returned to the attacker.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the destination and reject loopback, link-local, multicast and private ranges before connecting; re-apply the check after every redirect or disable redirects (`allow_redirects=False`); restrict the scheme to http/https explicitly; and prefer an egress allowlist or a mandatory outbound proxy over a denylist.

findings.title: The resource proxy copies the remote server's Content-Type onto a CKAN-origin response
findings.evidence: ckanext/resourceproxy/blueprint.py:71 sets `response.headers[u'content-type'] = r.headers[u'content-type']` and lines 74-77 stream the remote body into that response, which is returned from the CKAN route `/dataset/<id>/resource/<resource_id>/proxy` (line 111-113) - i.e. on CKAN's own origin. The remote server is chosen by whoever set the resource URL. Nothing in the handler constrains the type or adds `nosniff`, and the repository-wide grep for security response headers returns a single unrelated hit (ckanext/datastore/blueprint.py:115). Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD (both the destination and its response headers are attacker-chosen); FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD.
findings.impact: A user who can create a resource points it at a host they control that answers `Content-Type: text/html` with a script; the proxy serves that script under the CKAN origin, giving the same same-origin execution as the download-path XSS above, reached through a different handler.
findings.recommendation: Do not forward the upstream Content-Type. Pin the proxied response to a non-rendering type (or an allowlist that excludes text/html, image/svg+xml and application/xhtml+xml), add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and serve proxied content from a separate origin.

findings.title: Full API key or bearer token written to the application log on every API-authenticated request
findings.evidence: ckan/views/__init__.py:260-277 reads the credential from the `X-CKAN-API-Key` header, the WSGI environ, or `HTTP_AUTHORIZATION`, and then executes `log.debug(u'Received API Key: %s' % apikey)` before it is used for lookup at line 279. The value is the credential itself, unredacted and untruncated, and the interpolation happens eagerly (`%` on the message, not deferred formatting), so it is built whether or not the level emits. Triage: FP-04 partially HOLDS and the severity reflects it - ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl sets `[logger_ckan] level = INFO`, so on the shipped template this specific call does not emit; it does emit as soon as an operator lowers the `ckan` logger to DEBUG, which is the ordinary debugging step. FP-07 DOES_NOT_HOLD: an API key is a bearer credential.
findings.impact: Where DEBUG logging is enabled - a routine operator action - every API key and API token used against the instance is written in clear to a log that is typically world-readable to operations staff, forwarded to an aggregator and retained. Anyone who reaches the log authenticates as those users.
findings.recommendation: Remove the value from the message or log only a non-reversible fingerprint (first/last four characters, or a hash prefix). Add a redaction filter for the `Authorization` and `X-CKAN-API-Key` headers at the logging configuration level so no future call site can reintroduce this.

findings.title: Every request header, including Authorization, X-CKAN-API-Key and Cookie, is emailed on each unhandled 500
findings.evidence: ckan/config/middleware/flask_app.py:580-586 defines a logging filter whose `filter` sets `log_record.headers = request.headers` (line 585), and the handler's formatter at lines 605-612 renders `Headers:            %(headers)s` into the body of an `SMTPHandler` message (lines 594-601) sent to `config.get('email_to')`. `request.headers` is the complete header set: the session `Cookie`, `Authorization`, and `X-CKAN-API-Key` all appear verbatim. The handler is installed whenever `email_to` is configured (line 573-575) and fires at `ERROR` and above (line 604), so an attacker who can provoke any unhandled exception controls when it fires. TLS on the SMTP hop is optional (`secure = () if asbool(config.get('smtp.starttls')) else None`, line 592). Triage: FP-04 partially applies (requires `email_to`, hence medium not high); FP-07 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-08 not invoked - the control would have to be in this repository and is not.
findings.impact: Any 500 triggered while a privileged user is browsing - or while a sysadmin's API client is running - mails that user's session cookie and API key to the configured mailbox, over a hop that may be plaintext, and into a mailbox with a different (usually weaker) access model than the log.
findings.recommendation: Send an allowlist of headers (or a redacted view) rather than `request.headers`; drop `Cookie`, `Authorization` and `X-CKAN-API-Key` unconditionally. Prefer a correlation identifier in the mail and the detail in the server log.

findings.title: JSONP on the Util API returns viewer-scoped data, including private datasets, to any cross-origin page
findings.evidence: ckan/views/api.py:81-86 wraps any 200 GET response in a JSONP callback whenever `callback` is present in `request.args`, and serves it as `application/javascript` (line 86, `_wrap_jsonp` at 145-146). The action endpoint defends itself against this: ckan/views/api.py:292-297 drops `callback` from the data dict and sets `g.user`/`context['user']` to None, so an action reached that way runs anonymously. The Util API endpoints do not - `dataset_autocomplete`, `user_autocomplete`, `tag_autocomplete`, `group_autocomplete`, `organization_autocomplete` and `format_autocomplete` (ckan/views/api.py:374-469, routed at 519-532) build their context from `g.user`/`g.userobj` and return through the same `_finish_ok`. The data is genuinely viewer-scoped: ckan/logic/action/get.py:1503-1509 computes `labels = get_permission_labels().get_user_dataset_labels(context['auth_user_obj'])` and passes them to the search, so `package_autocomplete` returns the private datasets the *victim* may see. Authorization is ambient - `user_autocomplete` and `package_autocomplete` are authorized via `user_list`/`package_list` (ckan/logic/auth/get.py:203-204, 219-220), which succeed for a logged-in browser. No CSRF token, no Origin check, and JSONP is by construction not subject to CORS. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (I checked for an Origin check and a token on this path; ckan/views/__init__.py:72-97 only ever sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin and never gates JSONP); FP-07 DOES_NOT_HOLD (permission labels prove the data is not uniformly public).
findings.impact: Any page a logged-in CKAN user visits can include `<script src="https://ckan.example/api/util/dataset/autocomplete?incomplete=a&callback=leak">` and read back the names and titles of datasets the victim can see, private ones included, plus user names and full names via the user endpoint - a silent cross-origin read of authenticated content with no user interaction.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same defence the action endpoint already has to the Util API: when `callback` is present, drop the user from the context and serve anonymously. Better, retire JSONP in favour of CORS with an explicit origin allowlist, and never emit a JSONP body for a response whose content depends on the caller's identity.

findings.title: No CSRF protection anywhere, and the csrf_input() template helper is an inert stub that returns an empty string
findings.evidence: ckan/lib/helpers.py:3030-3032 is the entire helper: `@core_helper` / `def csrf_input(): return ''`. A case-insensitive grep for `csrf` across all .py, .html and .ini files in the tree (excluding tests) returns that definition and nothing else - no middleware, no token generation, no verification, no exemption list. Every state-changing web form therefore relies solely on the ambient `auth_tkt` cookie: `/user/delete/<id>` (POST, ckan/views/user.py:846), `/user/generate_key` (POST, lines 849-851), `/user/follow/<id>` (line 856), the dataset, resource and group edit and delete forms, and the sysadmin config form. This is the `WEB-27` shape - a control that is present by name and cannot fail - which matters because a reviewer who greps for `csrf_input` in the templates sees a control and stops. Triage: FP-01 partially HOLDS and is the reason this is medium rather than high: ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:61-66 defaults the auth cookie to `SameSite=Lax` (config `who.samesite`, line 99), which blocks cross-site POSTs in current browsers. It is a browser-dependent, single-layer control that a deployment can turn off by setting `who.samesite = none`, and it does not cover same-site subdomains, so the finding stands with reduced severity. FP-08 not invoked.
findings.impact: Where the SameSite default is relaxed, or the browser does not enforce it, or the attacker controls a sibling subdomain, an external page can make a logged-in user delete their own account, cycle their API key, follow or unfollow objects, or edit datasets and organizations. The empty helper also actively misleads: templates that call it render a form that looks protected and is not.
findings.recommendation: Add real CSRF protection - a per-session token issued by `csrf_input()` and verified by a `before_request` hook that fails closed for every unsafe method, with a short, explicit exemption list. Until that lands, either remove `csrf_input()` so its absence is visible, or make it raise, and document that `who.samesite` is load-bearing.

findings.title: No rate limiting or lockout on authentication, password reset, or the action API
findings.evidence: A grep for `ratelimit|rate_limit|throttle|lockout|login_attempt` (case-insensitive) across ckan/ and ckanext/ excluding tests returns zero hits. `UsernamePasswordAuthenticator.authenticate` (ckan/lib/authenticator.py:16-35) counts nothing and delays nothing on failure. `RequestResetView.post` (ckan/views/user.py:610-664) sends an email per request via `mailer.send_reset_link` (line 656) with no per-identity or per-IP budget, and its access check returns success for everyone (ckan/logic/auth/get.py:409-410). The only anti-automation control in the tree is reCAPTCHA (ckan/lib/captcha.py), and ckan/lib/captcha.py:11-14 returns early when `ckan.recaptcha.privatekey` is unset - so it is off by default, and it is wired only into registration, not into login or reset. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (I looked for a limiter in the app, in ckan/config/middleware/* and in the shipped ini template and found none); FP-08 UNKNOWN for a given deployment's reverse proxy, which is why this is medium - but the repository is the scope and the repository has no limit.
findings.impact: Unmetered password guessing against every account, and an unauthenticated email amplifier: repeated POSTs to /user/reset with a victim's address mail them an unbounded number of reset messages from the site's own SMTP identity, which also burns the site's sending reputation.
findings.recommendation: Add server-side limits keyed on identity as well as IP for /user/login, /user/reset and the action API, with progressive delay or lockout on repeated authentication failure and a per-address cooldown on reset mail. Enforce them in the application rather than assuming a reverse proxy.

findings.title: Password reset tokens never expire and are compared non-constant-time
findings.evidence: ckan/lib/mailer.py:214-219: `verify_reset_link` returns `key.strip() == user.reset_key`. Two defects in three lines. First, there is no expiry: the key is created by `create_reset_key` (lines 205-207) which stores only the value - the model column carries no issued-at timestamp (ckan/model/user.py) and no code path compares one - so a link mailed months ago stays valid until the next reset or the next `create_reset_key` call. `PerformResetView.post` does rotate it on success (ckan/views/user.py:748), but an unused link never expires. Second, the comparison is a plain `==` on a secret rather than `hmac.compare_digest`; note the same file's author used `passlib.utils.consteq` for the legacy password path (ckan/model/user.py:131), so the constant-time primitive was available. Entropy itself is adequate: `make_key` uses `os.urandom(16)` hex-encoded (line 211). Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (no expiry check anywhere on the path); FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD for the expiry half; for the timing half FP-10 applies - remote timing on a Python string compare is not a practical attack on its own, which is why the severity rests on the expiry, not on the comparison.
findings.impact: Any historical exposure of a reset email - a forwarded message, a mailbox compromise, a mail archive, a log of outbound mail - remains a live account takeover indefinitely, because nothing ages the token out.
findings.recommendation: Store an issue timestamp with the reset key and reject links older than a short window (an hour is typical); invalidate the key on first use whether or not the reset succeeds; and compare with `hmac.compare_digest`. Consider storing only a hash of the key.

findings.title: X-Forwarded-For is trusted unconditionally as the client address and recorded as the activity author
findings.evidence: ckan/views/__init__.py:136-139: `g.remote_addr = request.environ.get(u'HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR', u'')` and only if that is empty does it fall back to `REMOTE_ADDR`. There is no trusted-proxy list, no hop count, and no ProxyFix-style middleware configured in ckan/config/middleware/* - the raw client-supplied header wins whenever it is present. Line 172 then assigns `g.author = g.remote_addr` for anonymous callers, which is the value recorded as the actor for anonymous activity. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (no trusted-proxy configuration in the repository); FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD (a request header is attacker-controlled by definition); FP-10 applies - this is an integrity/attribution defect rather than an access-control bypass in the code as written, hence low.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller sets their own recorded address, so any attribution, per-IP analytics or downstream per-IP control built on `g.remote_addr` records or enforces against a value of the attacker's choosing. It also poisons the reCAPTCHA `remoteip` parameter (ckan/lib/captcha.py:18-19 reads REMOTE_ADDR, so that one is unaffected - stated so the bound is clear).
findings.recommendation: Only honour `X-Forwarded-For` when the immediate peer is a configured trusted proxy, and take the correct hop rather than the whole header; otherwise use `REMOTE_ADDR`. Werkzeug's `ProxyFix` with an explicit `x_for` count is the standard shape.

findings.title: API keys are stored and matched in clear text
findings.evidence: ckan/model/user.py:38 declares `Column('apikey', types.UnicodeText, default=set_api_key)` - the raw key, in a text column, with no hashing. ckan/views/__init__.py:279 authenticates with `query.filter_by(apikey=apikey).first()`, i.e. a direct equality match against that stored plaintext. This is a deliberate contrast with the password column, which is pbkdf2_sha512 (ckan/model/user.py:104-117), so the project already has the primitive. The newer JWT-based tokens (ckan/lib/api_token.py) store only a `jti` and are not affected. Triage: FP-07 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-09 DOES_NOT_HOLD.
findings.impact: Any read access to the user table - a SQL injection elsewhere, a database backup, a misconfigured replica, a support export - yields directly usable credentials for every account, with no cracking step.
findings.recommendation: Store a hash of the API key and compare hashes (the token mechanism in ckan/lib/api_token.py is the migration path), or deprecate the legacy `apikey` column in favour of the JWT tokens.

findings.title: No security response headers are set anywhere in the application
findings.evidence: The application installs after-request hooks for CORS and cache control (ckan/views/__init__.py:72-119, registered in ckan/config/middleware/flask_app.py) and sets no security headers at all. A case-insensitive grep for `X-Content-Type-Options|Content-Security-Policy|X-Frame-Options|nosniff|Referrer-Policy` across ckan/ and ckanext/ excluding tests returns zero hits, and the shipped ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl configures none. Triage: FP-08 UNKNOWN for any particular deployment's reverse proxy - stated rather than assumed, which is why this is low and reported as the amplifier it is rather than as a standalone defect.
findings.impact: On its own this is hardening. In combination it is what makes the two Content-Type findings above reach the browser: without `nosniff` a mis-typed response can still be sniffed into markup, and without a Content-Security-Policy an injected script has no second barrier. Absent `X-Frame-Options`/`frame-ancestors`, the UI is also framable.
findings.recommendation: Set `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a `Content-Security-Policy` in the same after-request hook that already sets cache control, and add `frame-ancestors`. Ship sensible defaults in deployment.ini_tmpl rather than relying on each operator's proxy.

findings.title: The upload size cap is enforced only after the oversize chunk has been written to disk
findings.evidence: ckan/lib/uploader.py:28-40: `current_size` is incremented at the top of each iteration, then a 1 MB chunk is read and written with `output_file.write(data)` (line 38), and only afterwards does line 39 test `if current_size > max_size`. The write therefore always precedes the check, and the loop admits `max_size + 1` megabytes before raising. This is the enforcement point for both declared bounds - `ckan.max_resource_size` (default 10) and `ckan.max_image_size` (default 2) via ckan/lib/uploader.py:97-108, called from ckan/logic/action/create.py:329-330 and update.py:333. Triage: FP-10 applies - the bound does exist and is enforced within one chunk, so this downgrades rather than disappears; FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD for the ordering itself.
findings.impact: Each upload can write one megabyte more than the configured cap, and the excess reaches the filesystem before rejection, so the cost is paid even for rejected uploads. Marginal on its own; it matters as an ordering defect in the one place the declared limit is meant to hold.
findings.recommendation: Compare the running byte total against the limit before writing each chunk, and count bytes rather than iterations so the cap is exact.
